references.text: The continuation of the story where Aaron and Hur support Moses' hands to keep them raised, ensuring Israel's victory.
Moses raises his staff over the sea, and God uses this action to bring salvation for Israel—a similar pattern of raised hands or staff.
The bronze serpent was lifted up, and those who looked at it were healed—a similar principle where looking up or being lifted brings salvation.
Joshua stretches out his spear toward Ai at the Lord's command, and the city is captured—a similar motif of an outstretched hand and victory.
Raising hands in prayer toward the Most Holy Place; hands lifted up in intercession and worship.
An exhortation to lift hands toward the sanctuary and bless the Lord—raised hands in worship and prayer.
The Lord's arm brings salvation when there is no intercessor—Moses' raised hands represent intercession.
The prayer of a righteous person has great power—Moses' raised hands were an act of intercession that influenced the outcome of the battle.
Paul urges men to lift holy hands in prayer everywhere—an echo of Moses' act of intercession.
Both illustrate how Moses' raised hand or staff serves as the physical means for God's supernatural intervention in battle.
A parallel showing how Moses' raised hand over the enemy triggers God's direct intervention to secure Israel's victory.
2 Chronicles confirms the principle that God grants victory, while Exodus 17 shows the specific act of prayer that triggers this gift.
